extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mathematical logic (advanced undergraduates / beginning graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Study of first-order languages/structures for the natural numbers (with symbols 0, S, <, +, ·, E), asking about decidability, axiomatizations, definable sets, and nonstandard models; includes quantifier-elimination procedures and characterizations of definability for NS, NL, NA and extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three key questions for a structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For each reduct/structure (NS, NL, NA, NM) raise: (A) Is the theory decidable? If so, what is a nice set of axioms for the theory? Is there a finite set of axioms? (B) What subsets of N are definable in the structure? (C) What do the nonstandard models of the theory of the structure look like?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three axes (decidability/axiomatization, definability, model-theoretic description of nonstandard models) as the primary criteria when evaluating or analyzing a first-order structure for the natural numbers. The textbook repeatedly returns to these three diagnostics for each reduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom S1 (zero has no predecessor)
rubrics_metrics.description: S1. ∀ x Sx = 0, a sentence asserting that zero has no predecessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the basic axioms included in AS (the axioms for NS). Use this to force that 0 is not a successor. This is used in analyzing models and ruling out loops that would make 0 a successor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom S2 (successor is injective)
rubrics_metrics.description: S2. ∀ x ∀ y(Sx = Sy → x = y). This asserts that the successor function is one-to-one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in AS. Ensures distinctness along successor chains and prevents merging of Z-chains; critical when characterizing models (standard part and Z-chains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom S3 (every nonzero has a predecessor)
rubrics_metrics.description: S3. ∀ y(y = 0 → ∃ x y = Sx). This asserts that any nonzero number is the successor of something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in AS. Together with S1 and S2, forces each nonzero element to have a unique predecessor, which yields the Z-chain structure for nonstandard elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom schema S4.n (no finite successor loops)
rubrics_metrics.description: S4.n. ∀ x Sn x = x for n = 1,2,... (the superscript n indicates S occurs n times). These sentences prohibit loops of finite length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The infinite collection S4.n (n ≥ 1) is used in AS to prevent finite cycles under successor; ensures the standard infinite chain beginning at 0 and that any nonstandard element generates a bi-infinite Z-chain. Important for classifying models of AS.

rubrics_metrics.name: AS (axioms for Th NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: AS is the set consisting of S1, S2, S3, and all S4.n (n = 1,2,...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AS axiomatizes the theory of (N;0,S) in the sense that Cn AS = Th NS. From AS one derives that any model consists of a standard part (0 → S0 → SS0 → ...) plus zero or more disjoint Z-chains (bi-infinite chains). AS is decidable and complete (Cn AS is complete), and available quantifier-elimination procedures operate relative to AS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of models of AS (standard part + Z-chains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any model A of AS has the standard points 0A → SA(0A) → SA(SA(0A)) → ... and possibly additional disjoint Z-chains (bi-infinite chains). Two models of AS are isomorphic iff they have the same number of Z-chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterization is used to show completeness (via Loś–Vaught test) and to reason about nonstandard models. It also shows there is no first-order sentence that says 'there are no Z-chains'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: elimination of quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory T admits elimination of quantifiers iff for every formula φ there is a quantifier-free formula ψ such that T |= (φ ↔ ψ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal criterion for a theory to have quantifier elimination; many decidability and definability results are derived by producing an effective procedure that, given φ, finds such a ψ. Equivalent restatement for Th A: φ and ψ are equivalent in the intended structure A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient check for quantifier elimination (Theorem 31F)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for every formula of the form ∃ x(α0 ∧ ··· ∧ αn), where each αi is atomic or the negation of an atomic formula, there is a quantifier-free ψ with T |= (∃x(∧αi) ↔ ψ), then T admits elimination of quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, it suffices to reduce existential formulas with conjunctions of (negated) atomic formulas to quantifier-free form; then use DNF and induction to eliminate arbitrary quantifiers. Use this reduction as the core step in quantifier-elimination proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier-elimination procedure for Th NS (Theorem 31G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: reduce ∃x(∧αi) where each αi is atomic or negated atomic. Terms are S^k u. Atomic formulas are equations Sm x = S^n u (or their negations). Handle cases: (1) if all αi are negations, replace by 0=0 (unsatisfiable/ tautological consequence); (2) otherwise solve an equation Sm x = t for x and substitute to remove x, converting other equations accordingly; result is quantifier-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete elimination algorithm yields decidability of Th NS and leads to the result that any relation definable in NS is definable by a quantifier-free formula; consequence: definable subsets of N are exactly the finite or cofinite sets. The method relies on the simple term structure in the language with only S and 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and decidability of Th NS (Cn AS = Th NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cn AS is a complete theory and equals Th NS; therefore Th NS is decidable (AS is a decidable set of axioms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness is proved using the Loś–Vaught test and the model characterization; decidability follows because a complete axiomatizable theory is decidable. The quantifier-elimination procedure gives an effective decision method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite axiom set AL for NL (axioms L1–L5 plus S3)
rubrics_metrics.description: AL is the finite set of six sentences listed: S3 (every nonzero has a predecessor) and L1–L5, where L1: ∀y(y = 0 → ∃x y = Sx); L2: ∀x ∀y(x < Sy ↔ x ≤ y); L3: ∀x x < 0; L4: ∀x ∀y(x < y ∨ x = y ∨ y < x) (trichotomy); L5: ∀x ∀y ∀z(x < y → y < z → x < z). (See page for precise formatting.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AL axiomatizes the theory of (N;0,S,<) (NL); from AL one derives S1, S2, S4.n etc. AL is finite (contrast with AS needing infinitely many S4.n) and is used to show Cn AL = Th NL. Use AL as the canonical finite axiom set when analyzing NL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier-elimination procedure for Cn AL (Theorem 32A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: reduce ∃x(∧βi) where atomic formulas are S^k u = S^l t or S^k u < S^l t; eliminate negations via L3/L4; ensure x occurs and only on one side, transform equalities like S^m x = t as in NS; if only inequalities remain, convert to lower/upper bounds on x and check gap conditions (existence of integer between bounds) to produce quantifier-free equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields quantifier-elimination for NL and hence completeness and decidability. The procedure essentially reduces existential constraints to simple comparisons of numerals and S-iterations, turning satisfiability into finite checks of bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of definable unary sets in NS and NL
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary: A subset of N is definable in NS (and also in NL) iff it is finite or has finite complement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantifier elimination to prove every definable unary relation is quantifier-free, hence ultimately equivalent to a Boolean combination of equalities S^k0 = S^l0, producing finite or cofinite sets. This provides a precise test for definability in these reducts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-definability of addition in NL
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 32D: The addition relation {(m,n,p) | m + n = p} is not definable in NL = (N;0,S,<).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: if addition were definable in NL one could define the evens, but the even set is neither finite nor cofinite, contradicting the definability characterization for NL. This is an expressiveness limitation criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presburger's theorem (decidability of NA)
rubrics_metrics.description: THEOREM 32E (Presburger, 1929): The theory of the structure NA = (N;0,S,<,+) is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decidability proof is based on quantifier-elimination after expanding the language to include congruence predicates ≡k. Practically, one uses the Presburger elimination algorithm to reduce formulas to quantifier-free combinations of linear constraints and congruences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion N≡ and quantifier-elimination algorithm (Presburger elimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand language by relations ≡2, ≡3, ... (congruence mod k). Procedure: (1) eliminate negations by rewriting ¬(t1 = t2), ¬(t1 < t2), ¬(t1 ≡m t2) into disjunctions; (2) express terms in normal linear form Sn0 + Σ n_i x_i; (3) uniformize coefficients of the quantified variable (multiply to common multiple p); (4) replace py by x and add x ≡p 0; (5) remove equalities by substitution; (6) reduce existence of solutions of linear inequalities + congruences to finitely many residue checks modulo the lcm M and finite bound checks; (7) produce an explicit quantifier-free disjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This effective algorithm yields, for any sentence, a quantifier-free equivalent in N≡ and hence a decidability procedure since atomic formulas reduce to arithmetic checks (numerals and congruences). Key practical steps: uniformize coefficients, reduce to congruences, compute lcm M, test M residue classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of definable sets in (N;0,S,<,+) (Theorem 32F)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of natural numbers is definable in (N;0,S,<,+) iff it is eventually periodic: there exist M and p > 0 such that for all n > M, n ∈ D iff n + p ∈ D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantifier elimination in the expanded N≡ (with congruences) and closure properties to show every atomic formula in one free variable defines either finite, cofinite, or periodic sets; hence every definable set is eventually periodic. Conversely every eventually periodic set is definable (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-definability of multiplication in (N;0,S,<,+)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 32G: The multiplication relation {(m,n,p) | p = m·n} is not definable in (N;0,S,<,+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: if multiplication were definable, the set of perfect squares would be definable, but squares are not eventually periodic, contradicting Theorem 32F. This gives a practical negative test for expressiveness of Presburger arithmetic.
